KEY MESSAGE 1... 
As of 3 PM, a cold front extends from extreme Southeast MI and
across Northwest OH. This front will sweep southeast across the
forecast area through this evening. There is also a lake breeze
boundary evident near the Lake Erie shoreline, especially
northeast of Cleveland. 

Isolated to scattered thunderstorms are expected to gradually
evolve along the cold front as it sweeps across the area. We may
also see a few showers or storms develop across southern
portions of the area ahead of the front on the nose of higher
theta-e air trying to advect in from the west-southwest, along
with along the aforementioned lake breeze. 

Warm and dry mid-levels, along with rather weak large scale
forcing, are negatives for storm development and have led to
activity being slow to get going so far. Jet support modestly
improves after 5 PM as a very subtle shortwave progresses 
across the southern Great Lakes, so do expect coverage and 
intensity of showers and storms to increase at least somewhat 
into this evening as the front progresses east across the area. 
Activity should exit to the southeast between 9-11 PM with the 
front. Overall, POPs range from 30-60% across the area this 
evening, mainly in the 30-40% range but briefly higher across 
the Wooster/Akron-Canton/Youngstown areas. 

Weak shear and the warm/dry mid-levels will make it difficult to
see organized/intense thunderstorms this afternoon and evening.
However, steep low-level lapse rates, moderate to strong MLCAPE,
and strong DCAPE can support a few microbursts/downbursts if any
more intense storms can play out. Confidence is low-medium.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
A cooler and drier airmass briefly moves in for tonight and
Sunday behind the front. There may be some patchy radiational
cooling fog in the "usual spots" early Sunday morning.
Otherwise, Sunday is expected to be rain-free until very late.
Highs will again be well into the 80s on Sunday, but dew points
will be about 10 degrees cooler than today. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...
The much-anticipated active pattern (some may call it a "ring 
of fire") is still on track beginning Sunday night. The pattern 
favors repeated rounds of storms with risks for both severe 
weather and heavy rain/flash flooding across the region through 
the first half of the week...however, would like to state quite 
clearly that these types of patterns feature plenty of 
uncertainty regarding the exact placement and severity of
storms, as each round of storms will modify the environment and
lay down boundaries that affect subsequent rounds. So the advice
at this time is to be prepared for unsettled weather through the
first half of this week, including potential for severe weather
and flash flooding, but to continuously check back for updates
as it's currently too early to have confidence in the details.

Aloft, ridging will be in place from the Rockies east across
much of the South, with a modest trough over the Northeast. 
This will put our area beneath a band of enhanced west-northwest
flow aloft for the first half of the week. At the surface, this
evening's front will lift back north as a warm front Sunday 
night and Monday, waiver across the southern Great Lakes through
Tuesday and into Wednesday, and finally push back south of the 
area late Wednesday or Wednesday night. Clusters of storms will 
be favored near and just south of the front, with some tendency 
in these types of regimes for clusters of storms or MCSs to dive
south of the front into the deeper instability. The forecast 
has elevated chances for rain and storms for several periods 
beginning Sunday evening or night across the area, though in 
reality storm chances will be occasional from late Sunday 
through Wednesday with a combination of various shortwaves and 
daytime heating modulating when risks are higher or lower. 

With the caveat that uncertainty increases farther out in time,
current consensus has a few potential window of elevated rain
and storm chances. An initial, weakening cluster of storms will
attempt to spread in from the west-northwest Sunday evening into
Sunday night. There is greater confidence in another cluster
spreading in late Sunday night or early Monday. Beyond that,
there's decent confidence in the next window for storms to
develop or move in will be late Monday and Monday night. 
Confidence decreases too much to identify additional windows 
with much resolution, but the front is not expected to sweep 
south until Wednesday or Wednesday night, so the forecast 
maintains elevated storm chances Tuesday into Wednesday.

South of the front, a combination of a very warm and humid
airmass beneath somewhat steeper mid-level lapse rates will
support moderate to strong instability Monday through Wednesday.
